- Avoid over-forecasting downward moves in the absence of negative sentiment; model tends to underestimate downside risk when sentiment is neutral or positive.
- When sentiment is negative (e.g., -1.00 or >0.20), model often underreacts to price drops, leading to delayed or exaggerated rebounds — adjust forecast to reflect stronger mean reversion or faster correction.
- Model frequently over-estimates short-term upward momentum after spikes, especially in 30-day horizon — cap upward revisions after sharp increases.
- In 30-day forecasts, model tends to underestimate true volatility and over-predicts mean reversion — apply a 5–10% upward bias to forecast if recent 18-day mean is above 65.00.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.00) and price is above 65.00, model often under-forecasts decline — add 1–2% downward adjustment to prevent over-optimism.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows a sharp spike (e.g., >68.00) followed by a drop, model tends to over-forecast the drop — apply a 3–5% upward correction to prevent overshoot.
